desc:
Call a non-empty subsequence of s balanced if every letter that occurs in it occurs the same number of times. For example "abab" and "c" are balanced, while "aab" is not.

Count the balanced subsequences of s. Two subsequences are different if they use different sets of positions, even if they spell the same word. Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007.

For example, s = "aabb" gives 11: the 4 single letters, the 4 subsequences ab (one a and one b), and aa, bb, aabb.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Enumerating subsequences is exponential. Fix the common frequency f that every used letter must have and count the subsequences for that single f.
For a fixed f, each letter independently either is not used, or contributes exactly f of its occurrences, in C(cnt, f) ways.
For a fixed f the count is (product over letters of (1 + C(cnt_c, f))) - 1, the minus one removing the empty choice. Sum over f = 1 .. max count, with factorials precomputed modulo 1,000,000,007.
editorial: Let cnt_c be the number of occurrences of letter c in s. Only these counts matter, not the order of letters, because a subsequence is just a choice of positions and being balanced depends only on how many positions are chosen per letter.

Fix a frequency f ≥ 1. Every letter either contributes nothing, or exactly f chosen positions out of its cnt_c, which can be done in C(cnt_c, f) ways. Choices for different letters are independent, so the number of ways (including the all-empty choice) is the product of (1 + C(cnt_c, f)). Subtract one for the empty subsequence and sum over all f from 1 to the largest cnt_c. With precomputed factorials and inverse factorials the binomials cost O(1), so the total is O(max count · 26) ≤ O(26 n) time and O(n) space.
